<reason>Side A won by reframing the debate from "precision vs. judgment" to "epistemic honesty vs. false certainty." A's introduction of confidence intervals and "inconclusive" defaults for calls within error margins directly neutralized B's "false precision" attack and exposed human officiating's hidden uncertainty. While B made stronger philosophical points about judgment being buried in calibration, A effectively countered that calibration is transparent and fixable whereas human perception error is invisible. A provided a concrete, workable mechanism for limited override (uncertainty flags plus physical plausibility tests) that B failed to fully dismantle. The clipped Rebuttal 1 was a significant execution cost for A, but A recovered sufficiently in later rounds to secure the motion.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange occurred in Rebuttal 2 when B challenged A on the 2mm offside example within uncertainty margins. A answered with confidence intervals and an "inconclusive" default, which B attacked as officiating moved to calibration. A's reframing of this as "honesty about limits" versus "confident ignorance" crystallized the core clash and gave A the cleaner path to victory.</best_rebuttal>
